raw_response.overlap_rationale: Both papers are readable full texts by overlapping author teams (Graham, Desai, and McFarlane 2013; McFarlane and Desai 2015) drawing on the same nine-month ethnographic fieldwork conducted across two contrasting informal settlements in Mumbai (four months per site, plus observation and unstructured/repeated interviews with residents, NGOs, and officials). However, their analytical samples only partially overlap. Study A empirically reports ethnographic fieldwork from only one of the two fieldwork settlements—Rafinagar (a non-notified, predominantly Muslim settlement in northeast Mumbai), specifically examining the late 2009 to March 2010 BMC/police water raids, water rackets, and post-raid water scarcity—alongside citywide media and policy discourse analysis covering Shivaji Nagar, Dahisar/Ganpat Patil Nagar, and Mumbai's bottled-water/leisure sectors. Study B analyzes the full two-settlement comparative fieldwork sample—both Rafinagar (approx. 4,000 households) and Khotwadi (an authorized, predominantly Marathi settlement of approx. 2,000 households in northwest Mumbai)—focusing primarily on moral economies and 'sites of entitlement' around public, private, and CBO-managed toilet blocks, drain cleaning, and water access. Study B explicitly cites Study A (note 22) when recounting the 2009 BMC/police water raids and temporary BMC water tanks in Rafinagar, and also notes a 2011 MHADA toilet block in Rafinagar Part 2 and a different ESRC grant code (RES-062-23-1669 vs RES-0360-7277 in Study A). Because the Rafinagar ethnographic fieldwork (including the pre-1995 slum cut-off rule, 2009 water raids, and temporary tank installation) is shared across both papers while Khotwadi (~half of Study B) and citywide media cases (in Study A) are unshared, this is a classic multi-site partial sample overlap with moderate double-counting risk for Rafinagar water findings.
raw_response.study_a_sample_and_data: Ethnographic fieldwork from a nine-month study of two informal settlements in Mumbai (four months per site), focusing empirically on one site—Rafinagar (northeastern Mumbai, adjacent to Shivaji Nagar in M-East ward)—covering the November/December 2009 water raids and January–March 2010 interviews with residents (e.g., Salma/Resident A, Residents B and C, Govind), NGO director Leena Joshi, and clinic doctor Ravindra Rathod, combined with secondary media and policy analysis across Mumbai (including Dahisar/New Link Road). Funded by ESRC (RES-0360-7277).
raw_response.study_b_sample_and_data: Nine-month comparative ethnographic fieldwork in two informal settlements in Mumbai: non-notified Rafinagar in the northeast (~4,000 households, 6 toilet blocks/76 seats; Part 1 and Part 2, noting developments up to 2011) and notified Khotwadi in the northwest (~2,000 households, 24 toilet blocks/180 seats). Data comprise participant observation and repeated interviews with residents (e.g., Salimbhai, Naina, Mumtaz in Rafinagar; Shobha, Lakshmi, Prabha, and garment workers in Khotwadi), municipal staff, NGOs, and CBOs regarding sanitation and water entitlements. Funded by ESRC (RES-062-23-1669).
